arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Dvoretzky argued Congress added actual fraud to the discharge bar in 1978.
He stated his interpretation gives meaning to that amendment.
Ms. Murphy argued Section 523(a)(2) applies to debts fraudulently induced.
Ms. Harrington argued the lower court erred in requiring intentional misrepresentation.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: Husky International Electronics seeks to discharge a debt. The creditor argues the debt arose from actual fraud. The lower court required proof of a specific misrepresentation. the side that brought the case argues this requirement is too narrow.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Husky wants the Court to reject the specific misrepresentation requirement.
Ritz wants the Court to keep the specific misrepresentation requirement.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Husky argues the statute covers any debt obtained by actual fraud.
Ritz argues the statute requires proof of a specific fraudulent inducement.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the scope of bankruptcy discharge bars. It determines which debts survive bankruptcy proceedings. Creditors rely on this standard to protect their interests. Debtors rely on it to achieve a fresh start.
